lesson.subtitle: Lesson 24 -- Checkpoint: Making the Case
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Rodrigo Marques de França | Lesson 24 -- Checkpoint: Making the Case

listenings.text: I have sat as an arbitrator in more than sixty cases, and what surprises young lawyers is how early I make up my mind. Not about the case, about the argument. Within the first ten minutes I know whether counsel understands where the burden of proof lies. If it is on them, and they spend twenty minutes attacking a straw man, a version of the other side's case that nobody has actually made, I start to worry for them. What I want is the opposite. Tell me the strongest thing the other side will say, and then tell me why it is still wrong. It was that habit, more than any brilliant phrase, that won the best cases I have ever heard. And please, no red herrings. I can see when a point has been added only to distract me, and every point that does not move the case forward makes me trust the others a little less. Short, substantiated, and honest about its weaknesses: that is an argument that stands up to scrutiny.

I coach university debate teams, and the first exercise I give every new student is an uncomfortable one. They write their best argument, then they swap papers and spend fifteen minutes trying to poke holes in somebody else's. Not only does it teach them to attack, it shows them where their own argument is weak. What they discover is almost always the same. Some of them had cherry-picked their evidence: three studies that agreed with them, and none of the ten that did not. Others had built everything on a premise that nobody had checked. And many had used a slippery slope. If we allow this, then that will happen, and then disaster. It sounds powerful until somebody asks, why would the second step follow from the first? My students must have heard me say this a thousand times. If you can't find the weakness in your own line of reasoning, your opponent will, and he will find it in front of the judge.

paras: Every lawyer has watched it happen. A colleague has the facts on his side, the law on his side and a client who is telling the truth, and he still loses the room. It is rarely the conclusion that fails. What fails is the line of reasoning that is supposed to lead to it. An argument is a structure, not a feeling: a premise that the listener accepts, evidence that substantiates it, and a conclusion that follows from both. Take away any one of the three and what is left is an opinion, however passionately it is delivered. The same is true at a dinner table, in a board meeting or in a family discussion about where to spend the holidays.

Arguments built in a hurry tend to fail in three familiar ways. The first is the cherry-picked fact: two numbers taken from a report of two hundred pages, which any careful listener can poke holes in. The second is the straw man, a weaker version of the other side's view, invented because it is easier to rebut than the real one. The third is the slippery slope, the claim that one modest decision will inevitably lead to disaster. Each of them can sound convincing for a minute or two. None of them stands up to scrutiny, and an audience that notices one of them will quietly discount everything else the speaker says.

Courts solve part of the problem with a simple rule: the burden of proof lies with the party making the claim. Ordinary conversation has no judge, but the rule still applies, and the best speakers behave as if it did. Not only do they bring evidence for what they say; they also make the case for the other side before they answer it, and they do it more fairly than their opponent would. Red herrings, however clever, are left out. It might seem a risky strategy, since it hands the other side its best material. In practice it is the opposite. An argument that has already survived its strongest objection is very difficult to defeat.
